facts.title: Lightning is hotter than the Sun’s surface
facts.body: A bolt of lightning heats the air around it to about 30,000 °C. The surface of the Sun is about 5,500 °C, so lightning is roughly five times hotter, but only for a split second.

facts.title: An animal with three hearts
facts.body: An octopus has three hearts. Two pump blood through its gills and one pumps it to the rest of the body. Its blood is blue because it uses copper, not iron, to carry oxygen.

facts.title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
facts.body: Venus spins so slowly that one turn takes about 243 Earth days, but it goes around the Sun in about 225 days. So a day there is longer than a year.

facts.title: Your heart never takes a day off
facts.body: The human heart beats about 100,000 times every day and pumps thousands of litres of blood around your body.

facts.title: Cleopatra and the Moon
facts.body: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing in 1969 than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza, which was built about 2,500 years before she was born.

facts.title: 54 countries, one continent
facts.body: Africa has 54 countries recognised by the United Nations. It is the second largest continent and has more than 1.4 billion people.

facts.title: Zero had to be invented
facts.body: Ancient peoples counted without a zero. In 628 AD the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote down the rules for using zero in sums, and the idea slowly spread around the world.

facts.title: The first computer bug was a real bug
facts.body: In 1947 the team working on the Harvard Mark II computer found a moth stuck in it. They taped it in their log book, and the word “bug” for a computer fault became famous.

facts.title: Which language has the most speakers?
facts.body: Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, but English is spoken by the most people in total, as a first or second language.

facts.title: Socrates asked questions
facts.body: The ancient Greek thinker Socrates did not lecture. He asked question after question to help people examine their own beliefs. This “Socratic method” is still used in classrooms and courts today.

facts.title: The smallest country
facts.body: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world, with less than half a square kilometre of land and fewer than 1,000 people.

facts.title: Why you can’t hear a shout in space
facts.body: Sound needs something to travel through, such as air or water. Space is almost empty, so there is nothing to carry the vibrations. Astronauts talk by radio.

facts.title: Bamboo: the fast grower
facts.body: Some bamboo plants can grow up to about 90 centimetres in a single day. That is nearly a metre of new stem in 24 hours.

facts.title: Saturn would float
facts.body: Saturn is mostly gas and its average density is lower than water’s. If you could find a bath big enough, Saturn would float.

facts.title: Babies have more bones than adults
facts.body: A baby is born with about 300 soft bones and cartilage pieces. As they grow, many fuse together, and an adult has 206 bones.

facts.title: Uganda’s big day
facts.body: Uganda became independent from Britain on 9 October 1962. Every year the country marks Independence Day on that date.

facts.title: Lake Victoria
facts.body: Lake Victoria is the largest lake in Africa and the largest tropical lake in the world. Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania share it.

facts.title: 0.999… really equals 1
facts.body: If you add 0.333… three times you get 0.999… But 0.333… is one third, and three thirds make 1. So 0.999… with the nines going on for ever is exactly 1.

facts.title: The first website
facts.body: The first website went live in 1991 at CERN, built by Tim Berners-Lee. It explained what the World Wide Web was.

facts.title: There are more than 7,000 languages
facts.body: About 7,000 languages are spoken in the world. Papua New Guinea has around 840 of them, the most of any country.

facts.title: Ubuntu: “I am because we are”
facts.body: Ubuntu is an idea found across southern Africa. It says that a person becomes a person through other people, so kindness, sharing and community matter more than being the best alone.

facts.title: A country with 11 time zones
facts.body: Russia is so wide that it spans 11 time zones. When it is morning in one end, it can be night in the other.

facts.title: Ice floats, and that saved life on Earth
facts.body: Most liquids shrink when they freeze, but water expands by about 9%, which makes ice lighter than water. Because ice floats, lakes freeze from the top and the fish below survive winter.

facts.title: Trees that share through fungi
facts.body: Scientists have found that fungi link the roots of many trees, and sugars and chemical signals can pass between them. How much trees really “help” each other this way is still being debated.

facts.title: The Sun is almost everything
facts.body: The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system. All the planets, moons and asteroids together make up the remaining 0.2%.

facts.title: Your brain is an energy hog
facts.body: Your brain is only about 2% of your body weight, but it uses roughly 20% of your energy, even while you sleep.

facts.title: Kasubi: a royal home of Buganda
facts.body: The Kasubi Tombs in Kampala are the burial place of the Kabakas of Buganda. They became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. The main building, made of reeds and bark cloth, was badly damaged by fire in 2010, and work to restore it followed.

facts.title: The Nile begins in Uganda
facts.body: The White Nile flows out of Lake Victoria at Jinja, Uganda. From there it travels more than 6,000 kilometres north to the Mediterranean Sea, one of the longest rivers on Earth.

facts.title: Pi never ends
facts.body: Pi, the number you get when you divide a circle’s distance round by its width, is about 3.14159. Its digits go on for ever without repeating, so no fraction can match it exactly.

facts.title: The first text message
facts.body: The first SMS was sent in December 1992 and said “Merry Christmas”.

facts.title: A flamboyance of flamingos
facts.body: Groups of animals have special names: a flamboyance of flamingos, a murder of crows, a parliament of owls, a pride of lions and a crash of rhinos.

facts.title: Occam’s razor
facts.body: When two explanations fit the facts, the simpler one is usually the better one to try first. The idea is named after the 14th-century thinker William of Ockham.

facts.title: Everest is still growing
facts.body: Mount Everest is 8,849 metres high. The tectonic plates under it keep pushing, so the mountain grows by a few millimetres every year.

facts.title: Diamond and pencil lead are the same element
facts.body: Diamond and graphite (the “lead” in a pencil) are both pure carbon. The atoms are arranged differently: in diamond each atom is locked in four directions, in graphite they sit in slippery layers.

facts.title: How bees give directions
facts.body: A honeybee that finds flowers returns to the hive and dances. The angle of her “waggle” shows the direction of the flowers compared with the Sun, and how long she waggles shows the distance.

facts.title: Astronauts grow taller in space
facts.body: With no gravity squashing the spine, an astronaut can grow a few centimetres taller in space. Back on Earth they shrink to their normal height again.

facts.title: Tooth enamel: the hardest part of you
facts.body: The shiny outside of your teeth, enamel, is the hardest substance in the human body. But it cannot grow back, so brushing and avoiding too much sugar really matter.

facts.title: Timbuktu: a city of books
facts.body: In the 1300s to 1500s Timbuktu in Mali was a famous centre of learning. Scholars came from far away, and its libraries kept hundreds of thousands of manuscripts.

facts.title: Rwenzori: the mountains of the moon
facts.body: Margherita Peak in the Rwenzori Mountains is Uganda’s highest point at 5,109 metres. The ancient Greeks may have called these snowy peaks near the equator the “Mountains of the Moon”.

facts.title: The birthday surprise
facts.body: In a room of just 23 people there is about a 50% chance that two of them share a birthday. With 70 people it is almost certain.

facts.title: M-Pesa changed money in East Africa
facts.body: M-Pesa was launched in Kenya in 2007. It let people send and receive money using ordinary mobile phones, and similar services are now used by millions across Africa.

facts.title: A sentence with every letter
facts.body: “The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog” uses all 26 letters of the English alphabet. A sentence like that is called a pangram.

facts.title: The Ship of Theseus
facts.body: If you replace every plank of a ship one at a time, is it still the same ship? Philosophers use this puzzle to ask what makes anything, or any person, “the same” over time.

facts.title: Antarctica is a desert
facts.body: A desert is a place with very little rain or snow, and Antarctica receives so little that it counts as the largest desert on Earth. It is also the coldest, windiest and driest continent.

facts.title: Sunlight is 8 minutes old
facts.body: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres every second, and the Sun is about 150 million kilometres away. The light you feel on your face left the Sun a little over 8 minutes ago.

facts.title: Elephants can “hear” through their feet
facts.body: Elephants make very low rumbles that travel through the ground as well as the air. They can feel these vibrations through their feet and trunk, which helps herds stay in touch from far away.

facts.title: Mars is red because it is rusty
facts.body: The soil and dust on Mars contain lots of iron oxide, the same thing as rust. That is why the planet looks red-orange, even from Earth.

facts.title: Blood cells have a short life
facts.body: A red blood cell lives about 120 days. Your body makes millions of new ones every second in the bone marrow.

facts.title: The first Olympic Games
facts.body: Records say the ancient Olympic Games began in Greece in 776 BC. They were held every four years, in honour of the god Zeus.

facts.title: Murchison Falls squeezes the Nile
facts.body: At Murchison Falls the mighty Nile is squeezed through a gap only about 7 metres wide and drops about 43 metres. The roar can be heard from far away.

facts.title: Fibonacci in the garden
facts.body: Start with 1, 1 and keep adding the last two numbers: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… Many sunflower heads and pine cones have spirals in these numbers.

facts.title: Everything is 0s and 1s
facts.body: A computer stores everything, even photos and music, as bits: 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte, and one letter on your screen takes one byte.

facts.title: Where the word “alphabet” comes from
facts.body: It comes from the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta.

facts.title: What you can and cannot control
facts.body: The Stoic thinker Epictetus taught that some things are up to us (our choices and effort) and some are not (the weather, other people’s opinions). Peace comes from focusing on the first.

facts.title: The deepest place in the ocean
facts.body: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean is nearly 11 kilometres deep. If Mount Everest were put in it, the peak would still be under more than 2 kilometres of water.

facts.title: A rainbow is really a full circle
facts.body: Raindrops bend and split sunlight into colours in a complete circle. From the ground the horizon hides the lower half, so we see an arch. From a plane or a hill you can sometimes see the whole circle.

facts.title: The baobab: a tree that holds a water tank
facts.body: A large baobab can store tens of thousands, and in the biggest cases over 100,000, litres of water in its thick trunk. It helps the tree survive long dry seasons.

facts.title: The Moon is slowly leaving us
facts.body: The Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres farther from the Earth every year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

facts.title: No two fingerprints are the same
facts.body: Fingerprints form before birth. Even identical twins, who share the same DNA, have different fingerprints.

facts.title: Mansa Musa and the gold
facts.body: In 1324 Mansa Musa, the ruler of Mali, travelled to Mecca with so much gold that it is said to have lowered the price of gold in Cairo for years. He is often called one of the richest people in history.

facts.title: Swahili reaches over 100 million
facts.body: Swahili is spoken by more than 100 million people in East and Central Africa. The word “safari” in Swahili simply means “journey”.

facts.title: The Ishango bone
facts.body: The Ishango bone was found near Lake Edward on the Uganda–Congo border region. It is about 20,000 years old and has rows of notches, one of the oldest known counting tools.

facts.title: Email is older than the Web
facts.body: Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email in 1971 and chose the @ sign to separate the user name from the computer name.

facts.title: Uganda speaks more than 40 languages
facts.body: More than 40 languages are spoken in Uganda. Luganda is the most widely spoken local language, and English and Swahili are official languages.

facts.title: A mind that grows
facts.body: Research by psychologist Carol Dweck suggests that learners who believe they can improve with effort tend to improve more. Making mistakes is part of how the brain builds new connections.

facts.title: The sea you can float on
facts.body: The Dead Sea, between Jordan and Israel, is so salty that people float easily on top of it. Its shore is the lowest dry land on Earth.

facts.title: The ice cream mix that surprised a schoolboy
facts.body: In 1963 Erasto Mpemba, a student in Tanzania, noticed that hot ice-cream mix seemed to freeze faster than cold mix. Scientists still study the “Mpemba effect” today, and they do not fully agree on why it happens.

facts.title: Giraffes and you have the same neck bones
facts.body: A giraffe’s neck can be two metres long, yet it has just seven neck bones, the same number as a human. Each bone is simply very long.

facts.title: A storm bigger than Earth
facts.body: Jupiter’s Great Red Spot is a giant storm that has been watched for well over 150 years. It is wider than the Earth, though it has been getting smaller.

facts.title: Your small intestine is about 6 metres long
facts.body: The small intestine is about 6 metres long when stretched out. It is packed into your belly in neat folds and loops.

facts.title: The wheel is a young idea
facts.body: People farmed for thousands of years before anyone made a wheel. Some of the oldest evidence of wheels comes from Mesopotamia about 5,500 years ago, where potters used them.

facts.title: Madagascar: a world of its own
facts.body: Most of Madagascar’s plants and animals are found nowhere else on Earth, including lemurs, which live only there.

facts.title: Algebra and algorithm come from Arabic
facts.body: The word “algebra” comes from al-jabr in a book by the scholar Al-Khwarizmi in the 800s. His name also gave us the word “algorithm”.

facts.title: The internet lives under the sea
facts.body: Most of the internet traffic between continents travels through cables lying on the ocean floor, not through satellites.

facts.title: Palindromes read the same backwards
facts.body: Words like “level”, “radar” and “civic” read the same in both directions. So does the sentence “Was it a car or a cat I saw?”.

facts.title: The Golden Rule is everywhere
facts.body: “Treat others as you would like to be treated” appears in many religions and cultures, in different words, all over the world.

facts.title: A country that is also a continent
facts.body: Australia is both a country and a continent, the only one in the world that is both.

facts.title: You are made of star dust
facts.body: Hydrogen and helium formed soon after the Big Bang, but heavier elements such as the carbon, oxygen and iron in your body were made inside stars and in exploding stars, billions of years ago.

facts.title: Why sunflowers face the Sun
facts.body: Young sunflowers turn their heads from east to west during the day to follow the Sun. This is called heliotropism. Fully grown flowers usually stay facing east.

facts.title: Our home galaxy
facts.body: The Milky Way, the galaxy that contains our Sun, has hundreds of billions of stars. Many of them have planets going around them.

facts.title: The smallest bone in your body
facts.body: The stapes, deep inside your ear, is about 3 millimetres long. It helps carry sound to the inner ear.

facts.title: Great Zimbabwe
facts.body: Great Zimbabwe was a large stone city built between about the 1100s and 1400s. The name means “stone houses”, and the modern country of Zimbabwe took its name from it.

facts.title: The Sahara is huge
facts.body: The Sahara Desert covers about 9 million square kilometres, roughly the size of the United States. It was green with lakes and grass about 6,000 to 10,000 years ago.

facts.title: 2 is the odd one out
facts.body: Two is the only even prime number. Every other even number can be divided by 2, so it cannot be prime.

facts.title: The QR code came from a car factory
facts.body: QR codes were invented in Japan in 1994 to track car parts. The square pattern can be read quickly from any angle.

facts.title: Many English words travelled far
facts.body: English has borrowed words from hundreds of languages: “safari” from Swahili, “pyjamas” from Hindi, “ketchup” from Chinese and “banana” from West African languages.

facts.title: Learning and thinking together
facts.body: Confucius taught, “Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.” Both studying and thinking about what you study are needed.

facts.title: The great river debate
facts.body: The Nile and the Amazon both claim to be the longest river in the world. Measurements differ depending on where each river is said to start, so scientists still disagree.

facts.title: Honey that lasts for thousands of years
facts.body: Honey has very little water and is slightly acidic, so germs struggle to grow in it. Sealed honey can stay good for a very long time. Archaeologists have reported edible-looking honey in ancient tombs.

facts.title: Only female mosquitoes bite
facts.body: Female mosquitoes need protein from blood to make their eggs. They find people by sensing the carbon dioxide we breathe out and the smell of our skin. Males feed on plant nectar.

facts.title: Footprints that stay
facts.body: There is no wind or rain on the Moon, so the footprints left by the Apollo astronauts in 1969 are expected to stay for a very long time.

facts.title: Skin: your biggest organ
facts.body: Your skin is the largest organ of your body. It protects you from germs, helps control your temperature and gives you your sense of touch.

facts.title: The printing press
facts.body: In the 1450s Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press with movable metal letters in Germany. Books became cheaper and ideas spread far faster.

facts.title: Wangari Maathai and the trees
facts.body: Wangari Maathai of Kenya started the Green Belt Movement, which has planted tens of millions of trees. In 2004 she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

facts.title: A shape with one side
facts.body: Take a strip of paper, give it half a twist and tape the ends together. You have made a Möbius strip: it has only one side and one edge. Run a pencil along it and see!

facts.title: Why passwords should be long
facts.body: A short password can be guessed by a computer in seconds, but each extra character makes it much harder. Three or four random words strung together are strong and easier to remember.

facts.title: Why we say “Mr” and “Mrs”
facts.body: These are shortened forms of “Mister” and “Mistress”. Writing a shortened form of a word is called an abbreviation.

facts.title: A story to ask “why”
facts.body: In many African stories, such as those about the clever hare or Anansi the spider, a small creature wins by wit, not strength. These tales teach ideas about fairness, patience and thinking before acting.

facts.title: Why seasons happen
facts.body: The Earth is tilted. When the northern half leans toward the Sun it is summer there and winter in the south. Near the Equator, as in Uganda, the seasons are mostly about rain, not temperature.

facts.title: Why the sky is blue
facts.body: Sunlight contains every colour. The gas in the air scatters short blue waves much more than long red ones, so blue light reaches your eyes from every part of the sky. At sunset the light travels farther, so the reds are left.

facts.title: Bwindi: home of gorillas
facts.body: Bwindi Impenetrable Forest in south-western Uganda is home to around half of the world’s mountain gorillas. It is one of the oldest and richest forests in Africa.

facts.title: Light from the past
facts.body: When you look at a star you see light that left it long ago. Some stars you can see on a clear night are hundreds or even thousands of light-years away, so you are seeing the past.

facts.title: Why you need to sleep
facts.body: During sleep your brain sorts and stores what you learned during the day. Learners who sleep enough usually remember more and concentrate better.

facts.title: Uganda’s nickname
facts.body: Winston Churchill visited Uganda in 1907 and called it “the Pearl of Africa” because of its beauty and rich wildlife. The nickname has stuck.

facts.title: Uganda sits on the Equator
facts.body: The Equator crosses Uganda, close to the road from Kampala to Masaka. Standing on it, you can have one foot in each hemisphere.

facts.title: A circle has endless symmetry
facts.body: A circle looks the same when you turn it by any amount, and has infinitely many lines of symmetry. A square has only four.

facts.title: Computers can’t really “think”
facts.body: A computer follows instructions very fast but only does what its program says. A programmer’s job is to break a problem into steps it can follow.

facts.title: Proverbs: wisdom in a few words
facts.body: Most languages have proverbs. In Swahili people say, “Haba na haba hujaza kibaba”: little by little fills the measure. It teaches that small, steady effort adds up.

facts.title: Most of the Earth is ocean
facts.body: About 71% of the Earth’s surface is covered by ocean, but humans have explored only a small part of it.

facts.title: Your phone is full of rare metals
facts.body: A phone uses dozens of elements, including tiny amounts of gold, copper and rare metals such as cobalt. That is one reason recycling old phones is so important.

facts.title: A leaf is a food factory
facts.body: Plants take in carbon dioxide and water and use sunlight to make sugar. This is photosynthesis, and the oxygen they release as a by-product is the oxygen we breathe.

facts.title: You are mostly water
facts.body: Water makes up about 60% of an adult’s body weight, and even more in babies. Drinking enough keeps your body and brain working well.

facts.title: The Nile civilisation
facts.body: Ancient Egypt grew along the Nile because the yearly flood left rich soil on the land. The Egyptians counted a 365-day year, which is the base of our calendar.

facts.title: Kilimanjaro: Africa’s rooftop
facts.body: Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania is 5,895 metres high, the tallest mountain in Africa and the tallest free-standing mountain in the world.

facts.title: The driest and the wettest
facts.body: The Atacama Desert in Chile has places where it has hardly ever rained. Others, like parts of north-east India, get more than ten metres of rain each year.

facts.title: Fish don’t blink
facts.body: Most fish have no eyelids, so they never blink. Their eyes stay clean and wet because they live in water.
